title: Avoid Using <div> Inside <a> – Violates HTML5 Semantics

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body:
### What problem are you trying to solve? Placing block-level elements like
inside an tag violates HTML5 semantic rules and can lead to accessibility issues, inconsistent rendering across browsers, and problems with validation tools. Why It's a Problem: 1. The tag is inline by default, and putting a block-level element like
inside it was not allowed in older HTML specs. 2. HTML5 relaxed the rules slightly (e.g., allowing block-level content if wraps flow content), but many linters, screen readers, and accessibility tools still flag this as bad practice. 3. It is better to use a or wrap only inline/phrasing content, or apply styling differently. Bad Example (Violates Semantics):
Click Here
 Good Example (Semantically Correct): Click Here Or, using a block element styled like a link:
Click Here
### What solutions exist today? 1. Use inline elements like inside If you want to wrap part of the text or add styling, use inline elements instead of
. html: Click here css: .highlight { font-weight: bold; color: blue; } ------------------------------ 2. Use a
or block element as a link with ARIA role and keyboard support If you need a whole block clickable but can’t use with block inside, use a
and add accessibility: html:
Click here (block div acting like a link)
- role="link" tells screen readers this behaves like a link. - tabindex="0" makes it focusable via keyboard. - The onkeypress handles Enter key activation. ### How would you solve it? Avoid nesting block-level elements inside . If styling or layout requires, wrap inline elements () inside . Only use ARIA role and keyboard handlers on non- elements when absolutely necessary. ### Anything else? - Accessibility matters: Using semantic tags properly helps screen readers and keyboard users. - SEO matters: Search engines expect links inside tags. - Avoid unexpected behavior: Nesting block elements inside inline ones can cause browser quirks. - Use linting tools: Configure ESLint/HTMLHint to warn about block elements inside . Analogy: Kitchen Items in Bedroom (Explaining
Inside ) If it’s your own home, it’s okay to keep kitchen items in the bedroom because you know where everything is. But: - It’s not a good way to maintain your home. - It doesn't look organized or standard. - If a new person or guest visits, they’ll get confused searching for things. Similarly, putting a
inside an tag is allowed by browsers, but: - It’s bad for maintainability and semantic clarity. - It breaks expected HTML structure standards. - It causes confusion for new developers, screen readers, and tools that expect cleaner code. This analogy helps explain why something might be technically possible but still discouraged for better code quality and future-proofing.
